items.abstract:
<jats:title>ABSTRACT</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>To investigate oral health in the fragmented human remains from the Punic necropolis of Monte Luna, Sardinia, and evaluate what dental pathologies reveal about lifeways and diet. Human remains from 227 individuals recovered from 70 tombs were analyzed, including 21 females, 16 males (> 15 years), and 59 non‐adults (1–15 years). The sample comprised 2362 teeth. Caries, antemortem tooth loss (AMTL), and periapical lesions were recorded and compared by sex and age. Caries prevalence was low but increased with age. In sexed individuals, males showed an age‐related increase in caries, whereas females exhibited caries across all age groups and higher AMTL rates in older adulthood. Oral health patterns are consistent with agro‐pastoral and coastal subsistence practices and reflect dietary traditions shaped by the environmental and cultural context of Punic Sardinia. This study presents the first comprehensive bioarcheological assessment of oral health in a Punic Sardinian population, providing insights into age‐ and sex‐related variation in dental disease. Interpretation of age‐ and sex‐related patterns was limited by small sample sizes and the fragmented nature of the skeletal assemblage. Analysis of additional Sardinian assemblages, combined with stable isotope, dental microwear, proteomic, and developmental stress marker studies, could further clarify long‐term health and dietary change.</jats:p>

items.title: Bioarcheological Insights From Fragmented Remains: Using Dental Health to Understand the Punic Necropolis of Monte Luna

items.abstract: by Lucia Martina Scalise, Maria Pia Morigi, Claudio Cavazzuti, Rosa Brancaccio, Enrico R. Crema, Marco Seracini, Stefano Benazzi, Emma Pomeroy Cremation is among the most destructive funerary practices. Over the past 30 years, radiographic imaging has increasingly been used to non-destructively extract information from cremation burials. Advances in scanners and imaging software have enhanced the quality of data retrievable through this method. However, scanning cremated remains, particularly when urned, presents challenges due to their fragility, size, material density overlaps, and the high cost of imaging equipment. These factors often result in low-quality images where distinguishing different materials becomes difficult and time-consuming. This exploratory research aims to provide and assess qualitative and quantitative information from tomographic images on burials’ taphonomy, biological profiles (sex and age at death), Minimum Number of Individuals (MNI) and thermal alterations to the bones and to evaluate a relatively simple segmentation strategy to analyse the spatial distribution of the remains in the vessels. For this purpose, 10 non-micro-excavated urns from the Middle-Late Bronze Age necropolis of Vicofertile (Parma, Italy) were scanned using Computerised Tomography (CT), subsequently micro-excavated, and the remains analysed to compare the information obtained from the two approaches. When extracted, data about the age classes, burial taphonomy, and heat-induced changes to the bones (e.g., fractures) were confirmed by the physical analysis, while the MNI, hypothesised to be 10 from the scans, was increased by one. Sex estimation was not possible from the scans. The vertical and horizontal distribution of the remains was estimated for cranial, long, spongy bones, upper, lower limbs, and trunk elements, with the vertical cranial distribution being the most accurately predicted category. Overall, the physical analysis proved essential to refine the results of virtual analysis and deal with the drawbacks of low-quality images. Despite the limitations discussed here, this research presents the largest systematic comparison of tomographic imaging and physical analysis of urned cremations to date, highlighting both the potential and the current limitations of CT-based investigation.

items.abstract: <jats:p>The fluvial deposits exposed at Stăuceni (northeastern Romania) have traditionally been assigned to the Miocene, due to the presence of cetaceans and seals. However, further investigation of the site has yielded additional fossils indicating a more complex depositional history of the site. Several fossiliferous layers, from the bottom to the top of the succession, yielded a mixed vertebrate assemblage including Miocene (kentriodontid and cetotheriid cetaceans, hipparion equids, sparid and merlucciid fishes) and Pliocene–Pleistocene (bovid artiodactyls, soricid eulipotyphlans, arvicoline, murid, sciurid, and spalacid rodents, lagomorphs, esocid and cyprinid fishes) taxa. The occurrence of Microtus (Microtus) nivaloides and Arvicola cf. A. mosbachensis supports a Middle Pleistocene age for the sedimentary succession, which contains reworked Miocene vertebrates, and rare Miocene foraminifers. The occurrence of Upper Pliocene palynomorphs suggests that Upper Pliocene units are also present at the very base of the succession. The mixed vertebrate assemblage from Stăuceni is not only significant for a better understanding of the local depositional setting, but also represents the only known site in Romania east of the Carpathians where Middle Pleistocene small mammals have been identified, thus providing important palaeogeographic information for this group. The occurrence of merlucciid remains is also unique for the East European Paratethyan realm, adding to the palaeobiogeographic importance of the site.</jats:p>
